ceb.title: The Sacrament of Confirmation
ceb.question: What is Confirmation, and why is it a separate sacrament if we already received the Spirit at Baptism?
ceb.answer: Confirmation is the sacrament that completes baptismal grace by a special outpouring of the Holy Spirit, sealing and strengthening the baptized for witness and mature discipleship. Its biblical basis is clear: in Samaria, though the people had already been baptized, the Apostles Peter and John came, laid hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit in a distinct action (Acts 8:14-17), and Paul likewise laid hands on the disciples at Ephesus so the Spirit came upon them (Acts 19:5-6). Scripture speaks of being sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Eph 1:13). This shows the early Church distinguished the gift of the Spirit in Confirmation from Baptism itself, ordinarily conferred through the laying on of hands and anointing by a bishop or his delegate. Just as the Apostles were baptized in a sense by following Christ yet needed Pentecost to be strengthened for mission, so Confirmation deepens and perfects what Baptism began, equipping the Christian to profess and defend the faith.

en.answer_full:
> "Now it is God who establishes us with you in Christ and who anointed us, who also put his seal on us and gave the Spirit in our hearts as a first installment."
> — 2 Corinthians 1:21–22 (NABRE)

Confirmation is the second of the three Sacraments of Initiation (Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist) and the one most often misunderstood in its purpose. It is not a rite of personal commitment, a graduation ceremony, or a Catholic Bar Mitzvah — it is the completion of baptismal grace, in which the Holy Spirit is given in a new and strengthening way, sealing the soul for the apostolic mission of bearing witness to Christ in the world.

---

## Biblical Foundation

### Acts 8:14–17 — The Samaritans

*"Now when the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the word of God, they sent them Peter and John, who went down and prayed for them, that they might receive the holy Spirit, for it had not yet fallen upon any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid hands on them and they received the holy Spirit."* (Acts 8:14–17, NABRE)

This text is the primary New Testament paradigm for Confirmation. Key observations:
1. The Samaritans were already validly baptized (by Philip)
2. Baptism was not considered complete without a subsequent impartation of the Spirit
3. The apostles (bishops) traveled from Jerusalem specifically to perform this ministry — indicating its importance
4. The laying on of hands is the ritual action through which the Spirit is received

### Acts 19:1–6 — The Ephesian Disciples

*"Paul laid his hands on them, and the holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied."* (Acts 19:6, NABRE)

Paul finds disciples at Ephesus who received John's baptism. He baptizes them in the name of Jesus, then lays hands on them. The two-stage initiation pattern appears again: baptismal water + laying on of apostolic hands = full initiation.

### Hebrews 6:2 — The Foundational List

*"...instruction about baptisms and laying on of hands."* (Hebrews 6:2, NABRE)

The author of Hebrews lists the *"laying on of hands"* as a foundational Christian teaching — alongside Baptism, resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. These are not peripheral practices but elementary doctrines of the Christian faith. The laying on of hands (the essential gesture of Confirmation) is placed at the same level as Baptism.

### 2 Corinthians 1:21–22 — Sealed and Anointed

*"Now it is God who establishes us with you in Christ and who anointed us, who also put his seal on us and gave the Spirit in our hearts as a first installment."* (2 Corinthians 1:21–22, NABRE)

Paul describes three actions: anointing (*chrisas*), sealing (*sphragisamenos*), and the giving of the Spirit as a *first installment* (*arrabōna*). These three concepts — anointing, sealing, Spirit-as-pledge — are precisely the three theological descriptions of Confirmation in Catholic theology.

---

## The Sacred Chrism: Anointing and Its Significance

### Old Testament Background

The practice of anointing with oil for consecration appears throughout the Old Testament:
- **Kings**: Saul (1 Samuel 10:1), David (1 Samuel 16:13), Solomon (1 Kings 1:39)
- **Priests**: Aaron and his sons (Leviticus 8:12)
- **Prophets**: Elijah anoints Elisha (1 Kings 19:16)

The anointed one in Hebrew is *māshîaḥ* (Messiah); in Greek *Christos* (Christ). Every anointing in the Old Testament looks forward to the one Anointed One in whom all three offices converge.

### Confirmation as Share in Christ's Anointing

In Confirmation, the baptized receive a share in Christ's threefold anointing:

| Christ's Office | Confirmed Person's Participation |
|----------------|----------------------------------|
| **Prophet** | Proclaims the Word of God in daily life |
| **Priest** | Offers daily life as spiritual sacrifice (Romans 12:1) |
| **King** | Governs self under God's sovereignty; works for the kingdom |

---

## The Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit

Isaiah 11:2–3 prophecies the Spirit resting on the Messiah with seven gifts. Confirmed Catholics receive a share in these gifts:

| Gift | Effect |
|------|--------|
| **Wisdom** | Sees all things from God's perspective |
| **Understanding** | Penetrates the meaning of revealed truths |
| **Counsel** | Guides moral decisions by divine illumination |
| **Fortitude** | Courage to live and defend the faith under pressure |
| **Knowledge** | Judges rightly about created things in relation to God |
| **Piety** | Filial love for God; reverence for the holy |
| **Fear of the Lord** | Awe before God's majesty; horror of sin |

**Fortitude** is the gift most specifically associated with Confirmation — the courage required for apostolic witness, the willingness to suffer rather than deny, the strength to live the faith publicly in a hostile environment.

---

## Church Fathers

> "After the water, the Holy Spirit comes upon the candidate... the flesh is anointed that the soul may be sanctified; the flesh is sealed that the soul may be defended; the flesh is shadowed with the imposition of hands that the soul may be illuminated by the Spirit."
> — Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, 8 (c. AD 208)

> "You were anointed as Christ's athletes... You received the spiritual seal... For you have been enlightened in your souls."
> — St. Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catecheses*, III.1 (c. AD 350)

> "The Holy Spirit is given through the laying on of hands of the bishop — this is the apostolic tradition which is observed everywhere."
> — St. Jerome, *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, 9 (c. AD 379)

---

## CCC References

| Reference | Teaching |
|-----------|----------|
| CCC 1285 | Confirmation perfects baptismal grace and gives the strength of the Holy Spirit |
| CCC 1293 | The anointing with Chrism communicates a spiritual character |
| CCC 1302 | Confirmation confers the gifts of the Holy Spirit for the Christian mission |
| CCC 1303 | Confirmation seals the recipient as a witness of Christ |

---

## Common Objections

**"Confirmation is just a Catholic custom — it's not in the Bible."**

The laying on of hands for reception of the Spirit (Acts 8:17, Acts 19:6), the anointing and sealing by God (2 Corinthians 1:21–22), and the listing of this laying-on of hands as a foundational doctrine (Hebrews 6:2) together provide a solid biblical basis. The *word* "Confirmation" is not in Scripture; neither is "Trinity." Both name realities that Scripture describes.

**"Young adults should choose Confirmation personally — it should be for adults."**

The Eastern Church's practice of confirming infants immediately after baptism (retaining the ancient unity of initiation) demonstrates that personal choice is not the theological heart of the sacrament. Confirmation is God's action, not merely the believer's commitment — just as baptism does not depend on the infant's choice. Confirmation in the Western Church of adults or adolescents includes adequate catechetical preparation; this is pastorally prudent without being doctrinally required.

---

Confirmation is the sacrament by which Christ breathes his Spirit upon the baptized a second time — not to repair what Baptism did defectively, but to strengthen and complete it, sending the confirmed into the world as his witnesses. In a society that constantly pressures believers to be silent, to privatize faith, to conform to the world's expectations, the gift of fortitude from the Confirming Spirit is not a nicety — it is a necessity.

objections.response: Scripture distinguishes a second, related event: receiving the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, distinct from water baptism itself. In Samaria, believers were "baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus," yet had not yet received the Holy Spirit until "Peter and John laid hands on them and they received the holy Spirit" (Acts 8:14-17). Paul does the same for disciples at Ephesus: after baptizing them, "Paul laid his hands on them, and the holy Spirit came upon them" (Acts 19:5-6). Confirmation is the Church's sacramental continuation of this apostolic laying-on-of-hands that completes Christian initiation.
objections.objection: Confirmation as a separate sacrament from baptism has no clear biblical institution — the New Testament describes only baptism as the rite of Christian initiation.

objections.response: Scripture does describe an initial gift of the Spirit at baptism (Acts 2:38), and also a further strengthening and sealing distinct from it: "it is God who establishes us with you in Christ and has anointed us, he has also put his seal upon us and given the Spirit in our hearts as a first installment" (2 Corinthians 1:21-22); "you were also sealed with the promised holy Spirit" (Ephesians 1:13). Confirmation is this sealing and strengthening for mature Christian witness, not a claim that baptism gave an incomplete or deficient Spirit.
objections.objection: Every believer already receives the Holy Spirit fully at the moment of faith or baptism (Acts 2:38) — a separate "sealing" rite adds nothing.
